title: K Lightest Pairs From Two Sorted Lists
statement:
You get two integer arrays a and b, each sorted in non-decreasing order, and an integer k. A pair takes one element from a and one from b; elements at different positions count as different pairs even when their values are equal.

Return the k pairs with the smallest sums, as [x, y] with x from a and y from b, listed from the smallest sum upwards. Pairs with equal sums may appear in any order among themselves, and when several pairs tie at the cut-off, any of them may be chosen.

k is never larger than the number of possible pairs.

examples.why: Sums 3, 4, 6, 7. Staying on a's first element would give [1, 10] (sum 11) as the third pair; moving to 4 in a is cheaper.
The two 1s in a are different elements, so [1, 1] appears twice.
k equals the number of pairs, so every pair is returned, in order of sum.

constraints: a and b are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Picture a grid where cell (i, j) holds a[i] + b[j]. Rows and columns are sorted. Where can the next smallest sum be?
Treat each row i as a sorted list: a[i] + b[0], a[i] + b[1], … Now you are merging many sorted lists and want the first k items.
Put (a[i] + b[0], i, 0) for the first min(k, n) rows into a min-heap. Pop the smallest k times; after popping (i, j), push (i, j + 1).

explain.intuition:
Lay the sums out as a grid: row i, column j holds a[i] + b[j]. Because both arrays are sorted, every row is sorted left to right. So the problem is "take the first k items when merging n sorted lists", the same job as merging sorted result pages from several servers.

A min-heap holds the current front of each row. The smallest front is the next answer. After taking it from row i, the only new candidate in that row is the cell just to its right, so push that. Only the first k rows can ever matter, because each of them starts with a sum no bigger than any later row's start.
steps: Push (a[i] + b[0], i, 0) for i = 0 … min(k, a.length) − 1.
Repeat k times: pop the smallest (sum, i, j) and add [a[i], b[j]] to the answer.
If j + 1 < b.length, push (a[i] + b[j + 1], i, j + 1).
pitfalls: Walking two pointers greedily. The next smallest sum can be in any row, as the first example shows.
Generating all n × m pairs and sorting. With 100 000 elements each that is 10¹⁰ pairs.
Pushing both (i + 1, j) and (i, j + 1) without a visited set. The same cell gets pushed twice and appears twice in the answer.

solutions.title: All pairs, then sort
solutions.idea: Build every pair, sort by sum, take the first k.

solutions.title: Min-heap over row fronts
solutions.idea: Each row i is a sorted list a[i] + b[j]. Merge the first k rows with a heap and stop after k pops.

followups: Return only the k-th smallest sum, with k up to 10¹⁰. (Binary search on the sum and count pairs with two pointers.)
Do the same with three sorted arrays.
lcTitle: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
